intro: Chrome for documentary filmmakers on Mac is mostly a research tool. You search archive catalogs, track down rights holders, and compare license quotes, often with dozens of tabs open at once. This page covers how to organize that work with tab groups, which Mac shortcuts to learn, and where Lazur fits in.
tldr: Group tabs by film, then by task: archive, rights, interviews, and filed pages.
Learn ⌘⇧A for tab search and ⌘⇧T to reopen a closed tab or window.
Ungrouping deletes the group on every device signed in to the same Google Account.
Start rights research early. Clearance can cost real money and replies can be slow.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask Lazur where things are, how to do them, or to draft a note.

blocks.text: What documentary filmmakers do in Chrome

Most of the browser work in documentary filmmaking is research. You search archive catalogs and database portals. You find the person who controls a clip, a photo, or a song. You ask for a quote and wait. Every step leaves tabs open, and every tab needs a home.

The archival research accounts we read describe the same pattern. One filmmaker spent a four-year period as the primary archival researcher on a single film. Some leads took months to revisit. That is a lot of tabs to keep track of.

items: Searching archive catalogs and finding aids for footage, stills, and audio
Finding the owner of a clip, photo, song, or interview
Requesting license quotes, then tracking replies and follow ups
Logging each source with its link, date, and what it said
Watching or listening to material, which takes time in any search system

blocks.text: Set up tab groups for one film, not one browser

Tab groups are the Chrome feature that fits this work best. A group holds related tabs under one name and one color. Use one window per film, then split that window into groups by task. Keep each group small enough to scan at a glance.

To make a group on your Mac, right-click a tab. Choose Add tab to group, then New group. Name the group and pick a color. Select the group's name or colored circle to collapse it. Select it again to expand it.

blocks.text: Name groups by the question they answer. 'Rights: music' tells you what to do next. 'Stuff from the library' does not. Good names matter more than colors, especially when you come back to a project after a week away.
Split by film before you split by task. The most common mess is two films in one group. When the edit locks, you cannot tell which quote belongs to which cut.
Keep your research tabs from disappearing
Closing a group does not delete it. Chrome saves the group to the bookmarks bar or the menu. To reopen it, click the Grid view icon on the bookmarks bar, or choose More > Tab groups.

blocks.title: Ungrouping deletes it everywhere
blocks.text: Right-click the group and choose Ungroup, then confirm. The tabs stay open on your Mac. The group itself is deleted on every device that uses the same Google Account.
If history and tabs sync to your Google Account, group changes sync too. That helps when you move between a laptop and a desktop. It also means one careless delete goes everywhere.

The Chrome help page does not say what happens to open groups when a whole window closes. Some third-party guides claim groups can vanish after a restart or a window close. We could not confirm that. Test with a throwaway group before you trust a long session to it. Check Chrome > Settings > On startup while you test, since some guides point to that setting.
Mac shortcuts for research in Chrome

items: ⌘⇧A opens tab search. Type the film name or the archive to jump to it.
⌘T opens a new tab for the next search.
⌘W closes the current tab. Check the group name first.
⌘⇧T reopens a closed tab or window. Use it after a bad close.
⌘⇧W closes the window. Plan for any groups in it first.
⌘Q quits Chrome. Save your log before you use it.

blocks.text: The help page lists no shortcut for creating, collapsing, or ungrouping a group. Use the mouse for those. For saved groups, go through the bookmarks bar or More > Tab groups, not ⌘⇧T. The help page ties ⌘⇧T to closed tabs and windows.
Searching archives without losing a week

Archive search is slow, and it often starts with nothing. The archival research account says searches often lead nowhere at first. Finding aids are usually less detailed than you hope. Some footage logs are 'incredibly sparse'.

Log your dead ends too. Write down each search term that fails. Then try the synonym, the decade, the place, and the name of the station or studio. A failed search saved in your log keeps you from repeating it next month.
Film often means reels, not files. The archival account's author had to borrow a projector and find a splicer to view 16mm reels. Put that step in your log, with the cost and the lab name.

Ask for people, not only pages. A study cited in the VIEW Journal article interviewed ten filmmakers. They preferred direct contact with archivists over formal finding aids. That is secondhand, since we did not read that study. Still, a short, direct question to a reference desk is an easy first move.

University special collections database portals: used in the same research
A Google search to find a rights holder's email address

blocks.text: A worked example: one archive clip, start to finish

Say you need a clip from a city's public works film. Search the catalog for the city and the decade. Add the best hit to the archive group. Open the item page and copy the call number, the format, and any access notes into your log.

Next, find the owner. If the page names a company or institution, search that name with the word licensing. Save the page where you found the owner in the rights group. Send the request from that group and log the send date.
If the quote takes too long, send one short follow up with the same details. Reuse the first message. Keep the second one to a few lines, and do not add new asks.
Find the rights holder and request a license quote

Rights holders are hard to find, and some do not answer. The Untold Stories study reports this for documentary filmmakers. One researcher's account shows the other side too. A rights holder there replied within 24 hours.
Build a rights trail as you go. For each asset, save the owner page and the email thread. Note the date and the quote. When you talk to clearance counsel, a clean trail saves time.

Write a first email that holds up on its own. Name the clip, the time range you need, the use, the territory, and the term. Ask how long the quote stays valid. Keep the message short enough to read on a phone.

blocks.title: Let Lazur draft, then read it
blocks.text: Ask Lazur to draft the request in your words. Read every line before you send it. Lazur types text for you, but you send the message, and you own what it says.
What clearance can cost, and why to check early

Clearance costs can climb fast. The Untold Stories study by Pat Aufderheide and Peter Jaszi interviewed 45 independent documentary filmmakers, mostly directors, in 2004. It reports rising clearance costs and cut or altered scenes. The figures are old, so read them as examples, not prices.

blocks.text: The BAVC Media study shows the same problem from the archive side. It surveyed 130 organizations that hold magnetic media. 77% of archive respondents said some recordings have questionable copyright or intellectual property status. That figure describes archives, not filmmakers. It tells you how often footage is hard to clear, not how often you will hit a wall.
The median archive in that study holds 3,500 collection items. 89% of those items contain material by or about historically marginalized communities. Plan rights research with that mix in mind.
Where Lazur fits while you work in Chrome

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It is not a plugin for Chrome, and it does not click buttons or operate other apps for you.

Three modes help most in a research session. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Ask for research, and Lazur runs it in its own Chrome tabs, then returns a summary and a report.
Dictation is a separate feature. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Use it to speak a source log entry into a document while your trackpad stays free.
Ask Lazur out loud, page by page

Short, specific questions get the best answers. Name the page, the thing you want, and what you plan to do with it. 'Help with this' is vague. 'Where is the request button on this page?' gets a circle and a label.

items: What does 'contact repository' mean on this record?
Walk me through the request form, one field at a time.
Draft a short note asking if this item has a second copy.
Remind me to check this portal again next Monday.
Hold fn and dictate what I just learned from the finding aid.

blocks.text: Mistakes that cost time and rights paperwork

items: Mixing two films in one window. Split by film first, then by task.
Ungrouping to tidy up. The deletion spreads to every synced device.
Saving pages with no date. Note when you checked each source.
Trusting a finding aid as complete. Ask the reference desk what is missing.
Starting clearance after the edit locks. Start during research instead.
Holding Lazur over unreleased cuts. Close those tabs first.
Waiting on one reply. Set a follow up date in your log the day you send.

blocks.text: Check your Chrome version before a big session

Chrome updates often. Google says there is a new Chrome update every four weeks. The releases.sh changelog lists Chrome 157 as the Mac Stable build, dated November 3, 2026, with Chrome 158 in Beta. Google's enterprise release notes still show Chrome 152 with a September 1, 2026 target. The sources disagree, so check your own copy.

Open Chrome > About Google Chrome to see your version and check for an update. Do this before a big archive day, not in the middle of one. The help page does not say how groups behave on restart, so test one group after you update.
Privacy notes for interview and archive work

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Memory of what you asked and did stays on the Mac.

That still matters for interviews, sources, and unreleased cuts. Close tabs that show private contact details or unseen footage before you hold ⌥ ⌘. Lazur sees what is on screen during that hold, so keep the screen clean for the question.
A simple daily routine for research in Chrome

items: Open the film's window and check that every group has a clear name.
Work the archive group first, since searches set the pace.
Log each useful page before you close its tab.
Move rights leads into the rights group, and date each request.
Close a group only after its log is complete.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ for help, and hold fn to dictate log entries.

blocks.text: End the session by checking which requests are waiting. Set a follow up for each one. Ask Lazur to add the reminder in Apple Reminders, and say the date out loud.
Where to go next

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Get it from the [download page](/download). There is a free trial with no credit card, and the [pricing page](/pricing) has plan details. For the Chrome side, see [Lazur in Chrome](/apps/chrome).

If you keep a shot or clip log in a spreadsheet, [create a dropdown list in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/create-a-dropdown-list-in-google-sheets) to track request status. To save pages into your log, [use the Notion Web Clipper on Mac](/how-to/use-the-web-clipper-in-notion).

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac, not a plugin for Chrome or any other app. It sees your screen while you hold ⌥ ⌘, then answers out loud and points at things. Background research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs.

faq.question: Will Lazur click buttons or fill in forms for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It drafts and types text when you ask. You do the clicking and the sending.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows or Intel Macs?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: Do tab groups survive a restart or a closed window?
faq.answer: The Chrome Mac help page does not say what happens to open groups when a whole window closes. Saved groups stay on the bookmarks bar or under More > Tab groups. Test with a throwaway group before you rely on it.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Lazur with unreleased footage open?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Still, close tabs with private material before you hold the shortcut.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. There is a free trial with no credit card, and it starts when you first open the app. The pricing page has the plan details.

faq.question: Can Lazur tell me whether I have cleared a clip?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can explain a term on a page or draft a request. Clearance decisions belong with your clearance counsel or insurer.
